summary:
TerraSync is an open-source, multi-sensor hazard exploration platform for Mexico. We integrated NASA GPM IMERG, Terra MODIS, GLDAS, FIRMS and EONET data with L-band SAR from NISAR and a historical ALOS PALSAR baseline, plus USGS and NOAA IBTrACS catalogs, into a single event store covering the 32 Mexican states and the 200 nautical mile EEZ from 2010 to 2027.
A calibrated supervised ensemble, validated with chronological backtesting, produces a state-level outlook for 2027, while an interactive timeline map lets non-experts scrub through 216 months of floods, cyclones, wildfires, droughts and earthquakes.
Because NISAR and ALOS PALSAR share the same L-band wavelength, backscatter is comparable across epochs, providing a surface-change screening layer. Mexico is exposed to two ocean basins, seismic subduction and seasonal drought, yet open satellite data remain hard to use. TerraSync harmonizes heterogeneous archives into transparent, labeled information (observed, supervised, proxy, non-confirmable) for researchers, risk managers and citizens.
details:
TerraSync is an interactive, open-source web platform that lets anyone explore Mexico’s natural hazards through time. We harmonized archives from NASA GPM IMERG, Terra MODIS, GLDAS, FIRMS and EONET, together with USGS earthquake and NOAA IBTrACS cyclone catalogs, and clipped them to the 32 Mexican states and the 200 nautical mile exclusive economic zone. L-band SAR from NISAR and a historical ALOS PALSAR baseline were reprojected and added as a surface-change screening layer. Since both sensors share the same wavelength, their backscatter is directly comparable across epochs. A calibrated ensemble of logistic regression, random forest and extremely randomized trees, complemented by Isolation Forest and autoencoder anomaly screening, produces a state-by-month outlook for 2027. We validated the models with a chronological backtest against independent catalogs, and a timeline map lets users scrub through 216 months, from 2010 to 2027, instead of guessing dates.

Open satellite data are difficult for non-experts to use, so our goal is to turn them into transparent, accessible information for researchers, risk managers and citizens. Every record is labeled by its provenance (observed, supervised, proxy or non-confirmable), so users always know what is a measurement and what is a model output. The interface is bilingual in English and Spanish, includes a plain-language Learn page, and can export filtered results to Excel.

We built the data pipeline in Python with h5py, pyhdf, netCDF4, Shapely, PyProj, Pandas and Dask, and trained the models with scikit-learn and PyTorch. The backend uses Django REST Framework, PostgreSQL 16, Redis and Docker, and the frontend uses React 19, TypeScript, MapLibre GL and Vite. It is deployed on GitHub Pages, Render and Neon.

TerraSync is also creative in how it presents data. The home page features an interactive 3D globe with the NISAR satellite in orbit, and the map uses a red-free palette to reduce alarm and visual fatigue. An optional sonification turns the patterns in the hazard data into music built on fifths, so users can hear how hazards change over time instead of only seeing them, which also offers a non-visual way to explore the timeline.

Throughout the project we prioritized spatial precision, using state-level clipping rather than a single national centroid, and scientific honesty, with leakage-aware modeling and explicit labels for what cannot be confirmed. TerraSync is a research prototype: the validation windows are small, and SAR currently has only two single-epoch scenes, so SAR-based hazard confirmation is future work. It does not replace official alerts from SINAPROC or CENAPRED.
